rv.q: So why five stars? Because it's so refreshing.
The 47th is an imagination of a future world.

'I know, I know, you hate me' declares the virtually unrecognisable Carvel at the outset, as he trundles on to Miriam Buether's sweeping thrust set in a golf cart. The 44-year-old actor is virtually half Trump's age, and yet the transformation is uncanny: there's the blonde wig and the fat suit, of ...
It’s gripping, funny, restless and ambitious, diving into the terrifying problem of leaders prepared to tear up democracy for their own ends.
Most marvellously, Trump's bonkers, bite-size Twitter philosophy is a perfect fit with Bartlett's modern take on Shakespearean verse.

Bertie Carvel’s Trump is alone worth the price of a ticket: not so much an impersonation as a reincarnation, as if Carvel himself has completely vanished and in his place something that seems barely human – a wax model perhaps – has been given palpable life.
It’s cartoonish fun, but it doesn’t offer much more to chew on than a Spitting Image sketch.
Goold brings his usual sheen to proceedings, yet can't hide the lack of meaningful substance beneath the theatrical polish.
The debate that unfolds is both fascinating and frightening, given more weight by the blank verse.
This is a performance that in itself makes this show worth seeing.
Bartlett’s audacity — plus the fact that Tunie, Wilson and especially Carvel never relinquish their grip on the audience — makes “The 47th” rarely less than entertaining.
Ultimately, Bartlett’s play, though vastly entertaining, neither offers fresh wisdom on the past nor grapples with the future.
It’s a shame that this promising play is so detached from its subject-matter but the creative team have decided to write about US politics without reading about it.
A severe, intense lack of depth pervades the piece.
Rupert Goold’s direction strikes just the right tone – his production fizzes with energy, tension and humour.

It's a playful fever dream about the corrosive impact of populism and social media on democracy, featuring a grotesquely lifelike turn by Bertie Carvel as the orange-hued panto villain who rocks up in a golf buggy with the taunt: "I know you hate me."
There's a perverse comedy to Trump and his interactions.

cn.t: Carvel's virtuoso Trump performance electrifies Bartlett's Shakespearean-styled election fantasy, but critics split on whether the blank-verse political satire has meaningful depth or just theatrical polish beneath its entertaining surface.
